note: Every name carries a signed edge_score on -100..+100. There is no call and no threshold: rank on edge_score and cut wherever you like afterwards, which is what makes the ranking question answerable at every k.

findings.finding: NSSF-adjusted NICS background checks for the three calendar months that are SPWH's fiscal Q2 (quarter ends 1 Aug 2026) ran May +3.2% (1,105,758), June +11.7% (1,123,006) and July +8.5% (1,061,883) YoY -- roughly +7.7% for the quarter -- versus only +3.5% (Feb) and +1.9% (Mar) in the fiscal Q1 in which SPWH delivered +2.1% same-store sales and +6.3% hunting/shooting; the two strongest months were published on 6 July and 5 August, after management reaffirmed FY comps of -1.0% to +2.0% on 2 June with visibility only through soft May.
findings.source_date: 2026-07-06 (publication date stated on page; URL path /2026/07/)
findings.adversary_note: The facts are correct and I verified them independently (July 2026 adjusted NICS 1,061,883, +8.5% vs 978,731; Q1 FY2026 comps +2.1% with Hunting & Shooting +6.3%). But NSSF-adjusted NICS is the single most-published public datapoint in this sector: the July release was carried on 5 August by Outdoor Wire, Tactical Wire, Ammoland, GunsAmerica, OutdoorHub, NRA Women and TheFirearmBlog, several with explicit 'gun sales stay hot' framing. Anyone who owns a firearms retailer sees it monthly, and the June release on 6 July was covered the same way. What is genuinely NOT drawn out is the link to SPWH's own Q2 estimate line, and I concede that: the 2026-08-30 StockStory/Yahoo preview has consensus revenue flat YoY (about $296.7m against $293.9m) and states analysts 'generally reconfirmed their estimates over the last 30 days', with no mention of NICS or firearms demand anywhere in it. So the data is loudly published and the SPWH implication is not. That is the 45-65 band, and I put it in the upper half of it because the publication is headline trade press rather than obscure, and because the magnitude is directly contested by the mix/margin findings below - the same accelerating demand is SPWH's lowest-margin demand lapping a 32.0% gross margin, so the EBITDA translation of a revenue beat is much smaller than the revenue translation. Separately, the NICS-to-SPWH mapping is looser than the finding implies in both directions: in Q2 FY2025 NICS was falling YoY while SPWH still printed +2.1% comps and H&S +4%, and in Q1 FY2026 H&S ran ~4 points above NICS. The series sets a direction, not a coefficient.

findings.finding: The $200 NFA transfer tax on suppressors fell to $0 on 1 January 2026, and NFA background checks have roughly doubled-to-tripled in SPWH's fiscal Q2 window (May 2026 146,551 vs 73,138, +100.4%; June 2026 166,677 vs 60,147, +177.1%; July 2026 130,013, +108.8%) -- and SPWH has been selling suppressors online through a 'Delivered by Silencer Central' drop-ship partnership since 12 March 2025, yet the words suppressor, silencer and NFA do not appear anywhere on its Q1 2026 earnings call.
findings.source_date: 2025-03-12 (date in URL path /2025/03/12/ -- deliberately checked, this is a 2025 release and predates the tax change)
findings.adversary_note: I checked the year on the source as instructed: the URL path is /2025/03/12/ and the Silencer Central drop-ship release is genuinely a 2025 document that predates the tax change - the hunter's date discipline is sound. But every macro leg of this is in the wire copy. The $0 NFA transfer tax effective 1 January 2026 is documented by SilencerCo, CMMG, Silencer Shop's dedicated '$0 NFA Tax Stamp Hub' and multiple trade explainers, and the NFA check surge was literally the headline on Ammoland's July write-up: 'July Gun Sales Rise 8.5% as NFA Checks More Than Double'. The suppressor boom as an investable theme has been written up against Ruger by name. What is unpublished is only the SPWH-specific arithmetic - and my primary objection is not that it is priced, it is that it is too small to matter. NFA checks are not suppressor units (they include SBRs, AOWs and other transfers), the SPWH channel is a third-party drop-ship where Silencer Central performs the transfer and ships, so the economics are a split or a referral rather than a full-margin retail sale, and SPWH has never quantified it in a release, a 10-Q or on a call. The hunter reads management's total silence on the Q1 call as concealed upside; the simpler reading, for a company that badly needs a good story and instead named hunting/shooting, fishing and personal protection as its pillars, is that it is not material. Even a generous share of a roughly $250-300m/quarter national suppressor retail pool is low-single-digit millions of revenue on a ~$300m quarter.

findings.finding: The 8-K filed 24 June 2026 (event 18 June 2026) pushed BOTH the senior secured revolver (resized $350m to $315m) and the $45m ABL term loan out to 18 June 2031, removing the 27 May 2027 revolver maturity that was still disclosed in the Q1 10-Q alongside $114.6m of borrowing-base availability -- so the balance-sheet mechanism that produced this stock's two extreme prints (-29.8% on 4 Dec 2025, +97.9% on 1 Apr 2025) cannot recur in the same form at this print.
findings.adversary_note: Two separate failures, and I want to keep them apart. First, on pricing: this was not a quiet 8-K. SPWH issued a press release, 'Sportsman's Warehouse Extends and Restructures Key Credit Facilities', and it was carried on 24 June 2026 by TipRanks, The Globe and Mail, TradingView ('Sportsman's Warehouse Refinances ABL Term Loan to 2031, Amends Revolver With Wells Fargo') and StockTitan, and posted on the company's own IR newsroom. That is wire copy, ten weeks before this print and well outside the 20-day window, so whatever repricing it deserved is in the base. Second, and more seriously, the causal premise is factually wrong. I checked what actually drove the two extreme prints. The -29.8% on 4 December 2025 was a full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance cut to $22-26m against roughly $34.6m consensus on a warning that consumer spending softened from mid-October, with Q3 revenue and EPS in line. The +97.9% on 1 April 2025 was a Q4 adjusted EBITDA beat ($14.6m vs $5.3m), a $27.3m net-debt reduction and a positive comp outlook. Both were guidance and EBITDA events, not maturity events. Extending a revolver to 2031 removes a date; it does not remove the mechanism that produced either move, and that mechanism is fully live tonight - SPWH is carrying a reaffirmed $30-36m FY EBITDA guide against -$8.1m in Q1, which is exactly the setup that produced December. So the finding, if believed, would cause a reader to narrow the tail at precisely the print where the tail should not be narrowed. I accept the fact and reject the inference.

findings.finding: The demand that is accelerating is SPWH's lowest-margin demand: Q1 2026 gross margin fell to 29.6% from 30.4% specifically because firearms and ammunition mix rose while higher-margin categories declined, Q1 adjusted EBITDA was -$8.1m against a full-year guide of $30-36m that is therefore entirely back-half-loaded, and Academy told investors on 10 June 2026 -- eight days after SPWH last spoke -- that it was 'tracking at flat comparable sales through the Memorial Day period' on 'persistent $4+ gas prices'.
findings.source_date: 2026-06-02 (Q1 FY2026 press release, thirteen weeks ended 2026-05-02, filed as 8-K Ex-99)
findings.adversary_note: I accept every fact here - I verified the 29.6% vs 30.4% gross margin, the -$8.1m Q1 adjusted EBITDA, and the $30-36m FY guide directly off the 2 June press release, and the back-half loading is arithmetic on that guide. That is the problem. All three legs are restatements of documents that were published and widely covered, and the guidance leg specifically 'restates published guidance', which my scale puts at 90-100. The Academy leg is also public: on the 9 June 2026 call (the finding says 10 June) management said sales through Memorial Day were up low single digits with comparable sales roughly flat and a 'little bit of a slowdown', and that gas prices are a headwind pulling roughly $17.5bn/month out of discretionary spend - written up by SGB Media as 'Academy Returns to Positive Comps, Sees Gas Prices Restraining FY Spend' and by MarketBeat/Yahoo in their Q1 call highlights. ASO is a multi-billion-dollar covered name, not an obscure source. The specific phrase '$4+ gas prices' I could not verify and it looks like an embellishment; what is verifiable is 'gas prices definitely are a headwind'. Note also that Academy's overall print was strong - comps +2.9%, sales +6.7%, raised the low end of guidance, stock up - so quoting only the QTD softness selects one side of a two-sided read-across. Decisively, the soft-consumer view is already in the numbers the market is trading against: consensus has SPWH Q2 revenue roughly flat YoY versus the +2.8% it just delivered, which is analysts embedding exactly this deceleration. The 15 points I withhold are for the framing that the FY EBITDA guide is now arithmetically dependent on a very large back half, which is true and is the live risk tonight even if every input is public.

findings.finding: NSSF-adjusted NICS for SPWH's exact fiscal Q2 window (May 1,105,758 / June 1,123,006 / July 1,061,883 = 3,290,647 vs 3,055,402 a year earlier, +7.7%) accelerated 5.4 points from the ~+2.3% of its fiscal Q1 (Feb +3.5%, Mar +1.9%, Apr +1.6%), the quarter in which SPWH printed +2.1% comps and +7.4% hunting-and-shooting.
findings.adversary_note: This is the same claim as SPWH-a#0 read off the same monthly NSSF series, and it should not be scored as independent information - see interactions. It scores marginally higher than a#0 because it adds no mechanism, only the arithmetic on the same three published monthly releases, and because one of its company figures is wrong: it states SPWH printed '+7.4% hunting-and-shooting' in fiscal Q1, whereas the 2 June press release and 8-K state Hunting and Shooting Sports same-store sales increased 6.3%. That is a small error, it does not overturn the thesis, and a#0 has it right - but it means the two hunters are not independently corroborating each other on the company side. The substance I concede is the same substance I conceded on a#0: the +7.7% fiscal-Q2 NICS aggregate against roughly +2.3% in fiscal Q1 is real, it maps to a quarter that ended 1 August 2026 and therefore lands squarely inside tonight's print, and I found no publication connecting it to SPWH's Q2 estimates - the 30 August preview has consensus flat and no mention of firearms demand at all. What holds the number at 60 rather than lower is that the input data is headline trade press covered by at least six outlets on 5 August, and that the EBITDA translation is contested by the gross-margin lap in b#1, which is the same demand read on a different line.

findings.finding: This quarter laps the highest gross margin SPWH has posted in the recent run - 32.0% in Q2 FY2025 - while the Q1 FY2026 it just reported came in at 29.6% (down 80bps YoY) with management attributing the contraction specifically to mix into lower-margin firearms and ammunition, which is precisely the category the NICS acceleration drives.
findings.adversary_note: The fact is right and I verified it independently, but not from the source given - the cited URL (accession 0000950170-25-080929) is the Q1 FY2025 press release for the thirteen weeks ended 3 May 2025, not the 4 September 2025 Q2 release, so the citation does not support the 32.0% figure even though the figure is correct. Q2 FY2025 was net sales $293.9m, comps +2.1%, gross margin 32.0% - up 80bp from 31.2% on healthier inventory and higher-margin fishing - and adjusted EBITDA $8.3m. Both halves of the comparison are therefore in company press releases that were reported at the time (the Q2 FY2025 release on 4 September 2025 across Globe and Mail, Yahoo, GuruFocus and SGB; the Q1 FY2026 release on 2 June 2026), and the claim is one subtraction away from them. That is 'published results restated'. I withhold 18 points because the specific framing - that this is the hardest gross-margin comp in the recent run and that the very mix now accelerating is what compressed margin last quarter - is a sharp observation I did not find written up anywhere ahead of this print, and it is the single best argument against the bull case in this brief. On size I am with the direction and slightly ahead of the implied magnitude: 32.0% was flattered by fishing mix and clean inventory, and a firearms/ammunition-heavy Q2 plausibly lands 100-150bp below it, which on roughly $300m of sales is $3-4.5m of gross profit - enough to neutralise most of the gross-profit benefit of the revenue beat that a#0 and b#0 are arguing for.

findings.finding: The 8-K filed 24 June 2026 amended and restated both facilities out to 18 June 2031 - the $45m ABL term loan and a revolver cut from $350m to $315m - so the near-term maturity wall the price appears to embed is gone, and Q1 liquidity was $116.7m against a minimum-availability covenant of the greater of $30m or 10% of the gross borrowing base.
findings.adversary_note: Same document, same event and substantially the same claim as SPWH-a#2 - it should not be counted twice. The refinancing was press-released by the company on 24 June 2026 and carried the same day by TipRanks, The Globe and Mail, TradingView and StockTitan; it is not a filing that only a diligent reader found. The added detail - Q1 liquidity of $116.7m against a minimum-availability covenant of the greater of $30m or 10% of the gross borrowing base - comes straight out of the 10-Q filed 2 June, also public. The load-bearing part of the claim is the assertion that 'the near-term maturity wall the price appears to embed is gone', and that assertion has no support I can find: with 23 contracts of total open interest there is no instrument in this name from which anyone can read what the price embeds, and the fact that the stock is 5.8% above its 52-week low ten weeks after the refinancing was announced argues the maturity date was never what the equity was discounting. What is discounting the equity is $22-26m of realised FY2025 EBITDA against a $30-36m FY2026 guide, -$8.1m in Q1, and a $1.18 share price - a leverage and earnings problem, not a calendar problem. Fact accepted, inference rejected.

findings.finding: BizLink (3665.TW), named in Credo's FY2026 10-K as the third-party manufacturer of its AEC products, printed accelerating record monthly revenue straight through Credo's fiscal Q1 (3 May - 1 Aug 2026): May NT$7.352bn (-0.4% MoM, +41.3% YoY), June NT$8.518bn (+15.9% MoM, +63.8% YoY), July NT$9.630bn (+13.1% MoM, +59.6% YoY, all-time high) — roughly +31% across the May-to-July span against a Credo revenue guide implying only +6.4% to +8.7% sequential.
findings.adversary_note: Every underlying fact checks out, and I concede the mechanism lands squarely inside this print's window (BizLink May+Jun+Jul maps almost exactly onto Credo's fiscal Q1, 3 May - 1 Aug 2026). But the finding is a read-across inference, and both halves of that inference are weaker than stated. First, the arithmetic: the hunter compares a May-to-July month-over-month chain (9,630/7,352 = +31.0%) against a quarter-over-quarter revenue guide. The like-for-like comparison against Credo's fiscal quarters is BizLink Feb+Mar+Apr = NT$20,784.6m versus May+Jun+Jul = NT$25,500.4m, i.e. +22.7% QoQ, and February is Chinese-New-Year-depressed (-14.3% MoM), which flatters the base; normalising February to trend puts it near +19%. So the claimed gap versus the +6.4%/+8.7% guide is overstated by roughly a third. Second, attribution: BizLink's own Q2 call on 2026-08-21 attributes the growth to HPC (+67% YoY, 42% of mix) and Capital Equipment (+52% YoY) and makes no mention of AEC, Credo or any specific customer. BizLink Holding runs at roughly NT$95bn annualised (Jan-Jul 2026 cumulative NT$53.74bn); Credo's entire AEC cost of goods paid to its contract manufacturers is on the order of US$200-300m/yr, so Credo is plausibly 7-8% of BizLink's consolidated revenue, and BizLink also serves NVIDIA rack-scale copper directly while Credo also uses Foxlink as a secondary manufacturer. A 22.7% move in the aggregate says very little about a 7-8% slice. Third, on publication: the monthly figures are TWSE-mandated disclosures and were reported contemporaneously by cnyes for May (June 2026) and June (July 2026), and BizLink is one of the most closely followed Taiwan AI-supply-chain names, so the data itself is public and monitored by every Asia tech desk. What I could NOT find, after repeated searching, is any article drawing the BizLink-to-Credo read-across, and the tape supports that: CRDO's 20-day run-up is -1.19% across the window containing the July monthly print (~5-10 Aug), so nothing was bid on this. That combination -- published and reported, not obviously connected to this print, magnitude genuinely contested -- is the 45-65 band, and I place it at the bottom of it because the US-facing connection is absent. I accept the fact and reject the size, not the sign.

findings.finding: Credo filed no Item 2.02 8-K — indeed no 8-K of any kind — between 1 June and 1 September 2026, even though this quarter has the same ~31-day quarter-end-to-print gap (ended 1 Aug, prints 1 Sep) as fiscal Q3 2026 (ended 31 Jan, printed 2 Mar), when on 9 February 2026 it pre-announced preliminary revenue of $404-408m against prior guidance of $335-345m nine days after quarter end.
findings.adversary_note: I verified the absence directly and it is factually correct: Credo's last 8-K of any kind is 2026-06-01 (accession 0001628280-26-039474), and the complete filing record from 2026-06-01 to today contains only Forms 4, 144s, the 10-K of 2026-06-15, a 13G/A, the DEF 14A and ARS of 2026-08-25 and an SD. No Item 2.02, nothing. So the fact stands. The inference does not carry the weight placed on it, for three separate reasons, and what remains is priced. (1) Observability: EDGAR is free, real-time and universally monitored, and the equivalent-calendar deadline for a pre-announcement passed around 10 August (nine days after the 1 August quarter end, matching the Feb-9-after-Jan-31 precedent). Every analyst covering the name has had three weeks to observe that nothing came. An absence that any reader can confirm in ten seconds is the definition of structurally known. (2) Base rate: Credo has been public since January 2022 and has pre-announced preliminary revenue exactly once in roughly eighteen quarters -- in the single most extreme quarter of its history, when revenue grew 51.9% sequentially and beat guidance by ~19%. The absence of a pre-announcement is therefore the modal outcome, and its entire information content is 'there is no 19%-scale blowout', which a consensus pinned at the guide midpoint ($470.7m against a $465-475m guide) already assumes. (3) The price history runs the wrong way for the implied sign: the one quarter Credo did pre-announce (+9.16% on 2026-02-09) was followed twenty-one days later by the worst reaction in the whole sample (-14.81% on 2026-03-02), while the two most recent quarters with no pre-announcement printed +1.28% and +7.40%. So 'no pre-announcement' has no demonstrated bearish signature in this name's own reaction record. I take the brief's point seriously that an absence is unfalsifiable in a way a positive disclosure is not: if Credo beats hard tonight, nothing in this finding can be shown to have been wrong, and that asymmetry is exactly why it should not be sized as though it were a disclosure.

findings.finding: Both mechanisms that could crash this print were pre-committed by management on the 1 June call: the CFO guided Q2 FY27 sequential growth as 'mid single digits, between our Q1 guide, and you can expect something similar in our Q2 guide' (i.e. roughly $490-500m), and guided FY27 non-GAAP gross margin 'to be broadly consistent with fiscal year 2026 levels' — whereas the -14.81% reaction on 2 March 2026 was caused specifically by cutting the Q4 non-GAAP gross-margin guide to 64-66% from 68.6% reported, not by revenue.
findings.adversary_note: Every element of this finding is verified and every element is published guidance. The 2026-06-01 release gives Q1 FY27 revenue of $465-475m and non-GAAP gross margin of 67.0-69.0% against Q4 FY26 actual non-GAAP GM of 68.3%; the call confirms 'mid single digit sequential growth in the first half', the CFO's 'similar in our Q2 guide when that comes', and FY27 non-GAAP gross margin 'to be broadly consistent with fiscal year 2026 levels' (FY26 was 68.1%). That is the top of the 90-100 band -- it restates published guidance, it is in the 8-K, the press release, the wire copy and every sell-side model, and consensus of $470.7-471.7m sits inside the guided range, which is the proof that the street has it. The attribution of the -14.81% on 2026-03-02 to the Q4 GM guide cut to 64-66% rather than to revenue is also correct, and was necessarily correct because the Feb 9 pre-announcement had already removed revenue as a surprise -- but that was extensively reported at the time and is not new. Separately from pricing, I reject the finding's logic, and this is a sign/inference rejection rather than a factual one. Guidance given in June is not a pre-commitment against a revision in September; it is precisely the thing that gets revised. The March 2026 episode is the counterexample inside the finding's own evidence: management had a standing gross-margin expectation and cut it, and the stock fell 14.81%. Saying the mechanisms were 'pre-committed' therefore removes no risk at all. And the +7.31 vol-point skew was set by a market that has had this guidance for three months -- so the skew is not mispricing the guidance, it is pricing the probability that the guidance changes. A claim that the skew is wrong because management already guided is an argument the option market has already heard and declined.

findings.finding: Both of Dell's closest server-assembler comparables reported the overlapping April-June 2026 quarter in mid-August with massive margin upside in the teeth of the memory spike - Super Micro delivered 17.5% GAAP gross margin on 11 Aug against its own prior guidance of 8.2-8.4%, and Lenovo's ISG posted a record 9.1% operating margin on 13 Aug against a ~4.6% consensus - which is the direct empirical refutation of the 'the assembler eats the memory bill' thesis that Dell's own preview coverage says is the whole question for this print.
findings.adversary_note: Both facts are correct and both were traded in DELL, by name, on the day. Super Micro's margin shock was NOT new on 11 Aug: SMCI pre-announced it on 21 Jul 2026 in an 8-K business update giving 15-17% gross margin against 8.2-8.4% guidance -- six weeks before the print the hunter cites, so the 11 Aug 17.5% was the confirmation of an already-disclosed number, not the disclosure. Lenovo's ISG print landed 13 Aug and DELL rose ~4% pre-market on it and made its 52-week high that session, with the read-across stated in the headline of the wire copy ('Dell Stock Gains as Super Micro, Lenovo Beat Expectations', Benzinga 13 Aug; 'Super Micro, Dell, and HP Jump After Strong Lenovo Earnings', 24/7 Wall St 13 Aug). That is the 70-85 anchor almost exactly: in the wire copy, and visibly in the price on the date it became known. The finding also agrees with the one thing the baseline measures cleanly -- a 25-delta skew of -9.3 vol points, upside paid, on a two-sided chain with a 3.3%-of-mid ATM spread. A bullish claim that agrees with the measured lean of the option market is agreement, not information. The steelman for the hunter is that DELL has since given the move back (-10.8% from the 52w high, -5.6% over 20 days), so the read-across is no longer in the price. I reject that reading of the tape: the give-back has identifiable, dated, Dell-specific causes -- a Morgan Stanley downgrade explicitly on memory chip costs, the 'memory boom splits the AI hardware trade' rotation (DELL -6%, WDC +5%), Aug 18 -3.3%, Aug 28 -3.7% after HP Inc's results -- i.e. the market absorbed the bull read-across and was then handed better evidence. A price falling on subsequent information does not un-price the prior information. Where I concede ground: the *quantified* size of the Lenovo beat (9.1% ISG operating margin against a ~4.6% sell-side average, sourced off UBS 4.0% / CLSA 5.2% / JPM 4.8% / MS 4.5%) is only laid out in an obscure outlet (BigGo Finance), not in Western wire copy, and that specific arithmetic is the genuinely under-drawn part. Separately, the hunter's mechanism is weaker than stated: SMCI's own filing attributes the margin upside 'primarily to a favorable customer and product mix', not to passing component-cost inflation through. So I accept the facts, accept the sign, and reject the novelty and part of the mechanism.

findings.finding: IDC's calendar-Q2 2026 PC data, covering two of the three months of Dell's fiscal Q2, shows the memory shortage working as a pricing-power event rather than a margin event for OEMs - shipments fell 4.9% to 68.2m units and Dell fell 5% to 9.3m while industry revenue rose, with comparable-line prices up 20-40% year over year and IDC stating vendors 'are pushing through price increases faster than demand is dropping'; Dell held share at 13.6%.
findings.adversary_note: This is the highest-priced of the two and the one where I also reject the sign. Every number in it was published on IDC's release day and syndicated across dozens of outlets in the week of 8-14 July 2026 -- 68.2m units, -4.9%, Dell 9.3m and -5%, share 'practically stable at 13.6 percent', and the revenue-up-on-units-down dynamic phrased as 'vendors' revenues are rising because price increases are being implemented faster than demand is falling'. That last clause is not a buried implication the hunter drew out; it is the headline of the hunter's own cited source (PC Gamer) and it is in the body of Igor's Lab on 13 Jul, 9to5Mac on 8 Jul, Asymco on 14 Jul and Electronics Weekly. When the finding's conclusion is the title of the article the finding cites, priced_in is near the top of the range. Two further objections. First, size: the '20-40% year over year' comparable-line price figure does not reconcile with the sources -- IDC's own PCD forecast is ASPs +18.3% for 2026, Igor's Lab cites Gartner at +17% average PC prices, and the vendor list-price warnings reported for H2 2026 are 15-20%. I accept the direction of pricing power and reject the magnitude as roughly double what the record supports. Second, and more seriously, the sign: the closest and freshest comparable points the other way and has already been traded in DELL. HP Inc reported fiscal Q3 on 26-27 Aug 2026 for a quarter ended 31 July -- a three-of-three-month overlap with Dell's fiscal Q2, against IDC's two-of-three -- and Personal Systems operating margin came in at 4.6%, DOWN from 5.4%, with the company stating that higher commodity costs 'more than offset repricing and cost reductions', PC units -16%, and no margin recovery expected until fiscal 2027. That is a direct, same-window, same-product refutation of 'pricing-power event rather than a margin event for OEMs', it is eight weeks newer than the IDC data, and DELL fell 3.7% on 28 Aug in its wake. So the market has not merely seen this finding; it has seen it, then seen it superseded. Finally, the mechanism is small even if right: CSG is roughly a quarter to a third of the ~$45bn consensus revenue line for this print and much less of operating income, and the AI server line is what a 9.29% implied move is being paid for. A 100bp CSG margin swing is not a 9% stock.

findings.finding: FuelCell's own careers site right now shows 61 of its 80 open requisitions at the Torrington cell plant and, critically, an entire third shift being staffed end-to-end -- Supervisor Tape Casting (Third Shift), Sheet Metal Supervisor (Third Shift), Warehouse Supervisor (Third Shift), Material Handler (Third Shift), QA Inspector Manufacturing (Third Shift), EH&S Specialist (Third Shift), Facility Tech (Third Shift), Janitor (Third Shift) and Security Officer (3rd Shift), plus a parallel second-shift set -- i.e. a 24/7 line being commissioned, not incremental backfill.
findings.adversary_note: The facts check out — I independently confirmed 61 of 80 open requisitions in Torrington and all nine of the cited third-shift titles exist on the careers site — but the INFERENCE is the consensus story, not new information, and two verifiable details break it. (1) The ramp itself is in the wire copy: on 2026-06-08 FuelCell publicly raised its Torrington capacity plan from 350 to 500 MW/yr at $200-275m capex, disclosed that a high-volume tape caster install had begun and a new conditioning room was commissioned, and reiterated the 100 MW-annualised EBITDA-breakeven target; CBIA (2026-06-11) and DCD carried it. Mass hiring at that plant is the mechanical footprint of an announced program, not a discovery. (2) The postings are not 'right now' — the Supervisor, Tape Casting (Third Shift) requisition has been live on LinkedIn for ~2 months (posted ~late June 2026) and shows a careers-site posted date of Aug 15, 2026, i.e. it is a REPOST of an unfilled req. A two-month-old, reposted third-shift supervisor opening is evidence the third shift is not running, which is the opposite of 'a line being commissioned.' (3) The shift designations do not support the inference the hunter draws from them: the 'Facility Tech (Third Shift)' posting states, verbatim, 'The hours for this position are M-F 3:30 pm to 11:30 pm' — identical to the site's own second-shift Process Operator schedule. At least one of the nine cited 'third shift' titles is a mislabelled second shift, and 'Supervisor, Tape Casting (Third Shift)' and 'Security Officer (3rd Shift)' state no clock hours at all. Janitor and Security Officer coverage is also consistent with a two-year construction site rather than a 24/7 production line. (4) Timing: the third-shift reqs I could date are Aug 4 and Aug 15, 2026, i.e. AFTER the quarter ended 2026-07-31, so they cannot show up in the printed quarter; and to the extent shift staffing does hit the P&L it is a near-term cost drag on a $35.6m-revenue quarter with negative product gross margin, so even the sign is contested. What I concede: no analyst note, wire story or company release has drawn out the shift build-out explicitly, the aggregator indexing (ZipRecruiter/Indeed/rejobs/LinkedIn) is genuinely obscure, and the put skew of +11.64 vol points says the market is not paying for a ramp surprise. That is why this is 55 and not 85.

findings.finding: Homer John Livingston III, who only became a FuelCell director on 19 May 2026, bought 26,343 shares in the open market on 16 July 2026 at a weighted-average $18.79 (about $495k, transaction code P, direct) -- an actual cash purchase at a company where every other recent insider line is a director-fee stock grant or a 10b5-1 sale.
findings.adversary_note: The Form 4 is exactly as described — I verified reporting person Homer John Livingston III, Director, transaction date 2026-07-16, code P, 26,343 shares at a $18.7893 weighted average (range $18.71-$18.79), direct, 26,343 shares held after — so nothing here is factually wrong. It is also the single most mechanically-syndicated disclosure type in the market: GuruFocus published it on 2026-07-20, the day the Form 4 was filed, and TipRanks and Quiver Quantitative both ran it. Six weeks of public availability on every insider screen is the definition of in the price. On base rates, a single first-time director purchase of ~$495k — against ~78.3m shares outstanding post the July offering, i.e. about 0.03% of the company — has close to no predictive power for the next earnings reaction, and the tape says so directly: the stock has fallen from $18.79 to $16.72 since the buy, so the purchase is 11% underwater and the market has already overwhelmed it. Context makes it weaker still, not stronger: he bought nine days after the $225m offering priced at $21.00 on 2026-07-07, which is the textbook moment for a newly-seated director to demonstrate alignment below the deal price, and he bought two weeks before quarter-end, when a director seated on 2026-05-19 would have had little quarter-specific knowledge. I accept the fact and reject the size, not the sign.

findings.finding: The Fit Energy CEPA's only alignment mechanism -- 12,000,000 warrant shares in three 4m tranches, each vesting only on FuelCell receiving a non-refundable deposit equal to 16% of the order value for the next 100 MW -- is struck at $26.44, now 58% above the $16.72 spot, and in the ten weeks since signing there has been no 8-K, no press release, no named data-centre site and no phase election; FuelCell's press-release feed shows nothing operational since 9 July, against management's own commitment to convert submitted proposals into contracted backlog 'within this fiscal year' (FY ends 31 October).
findings.adversary_note: Every fact checks out against the 8-K: 12,000,000 warrant shares in three 4,000,000 tranches, $26.44 strike, first tranche vesting only on a non-refundable deposit equal to 16% of the order value for the 100 MW Phase 1, executed 2026-06-22. And I confirm the news drought — the investor-relations feed shows nothing after 'Siemens and FuelCell Energy Collaborate' on 2026-07-09 until the 2026-08-25 conference-call notice. But almost none of this is hidden. The strike is in a public 8-K and the spot is on the tape, so '58% above spot' is arithmetic anyone can do; the absence of news is the most visible fact about the name — a stock with no press release for seven weeks, down 25.67% in 20 days, carrying the most bid put skew of the day at +11.64 vol points and a 'downside paid' lean, is a market that has already marked the Fit Energy optionality down toward zero. Benzinga wrote precisely this thesis in August ('FuelCell Pullback Deepens as Investors Weigh Data Center Promise Against Near-Term Risks'). Two things also make the bear framing harsher than the documents support: the 2026-06-23 announcement states Fit made an immediate deposit for an initial 30 MW with deliveries beginning later this year, so Phase 0 is firm and not silence; and the unvested warrants only cancel 24 months after issuance, so ten weeks without a Phase 1 election is well inside the contractual clock. The 'within this fiscal year' quote is real and I verified it on the Q2 call, but FY ends 2026-10-31 — two months after this print — so a missed conversion cannot be scored at this print, only worried about, and worrying about it is what the skew is already paying for. Finally, an absence is genuinely unfalsifiable in the way the brief warns: I can confirm no 8-K exists, but I cannot distinguish 'no deal' from 'deal not yet announceable', and the market cannot either, which is exactly why it is already in the discount rather than being a discovery.

findings.finding: CXM's own five prior prints moved +5.96%, -10.00%, +3.05%, +6.05%, -3.03% (close before to close of the print day, all pre-open releases) and the sign is conditioned on the run-in: the only double-digit decline, 2025-09-03, was the print it entered at $8.60 near its 52-week high, which is the same setup as today at $7.94-8.21 after +22.6% in 20 days.
findings.adversary_note: I independently reproduced two of the five moves from raw Yahoo daily bars and they are exact: 2025-09-02 close 8.60 -> 2025-09-03 close 7.74 = -10.00%, and 2026-06-02 close 5.62 -> 2026-06-03 close 5.45 = -3.03%. So the factual half is right, and it is also the single most public thing about this company: any participant with a chart has CXM's reaction history, and the only reason the baseline lacks it is a former-name filter bug the baseline itself flags. The conditioning claim, which is the only part that could be information, is factually WRONG rather than merely overfit. The showcase print did not follow a run-up: 20 sessions before 2025-09-02 the stock closed 8.87 (2025-08-04), so the run-in into the -10% print was -3.0%, not positive, and the stock was 4.8% BELOW its own 2025-08-06 high of 9.03 rather than 'near its 52-week high after a run.' Today's setup (+22.6% in 20 days, 7.5% below the 52w high) is therefore the opposite of the 2025-09-03 run-in on the dimension the finding names. Moreover the -10% has an identified idiosyncratic cause disclosed on that call: CFO Manish Saran's departure. n=1, and the one observation points the other way.

findings.finding: Sprinklr's FY27 non-GAAP operating income guide of $139-141m requires H2 operating income of ~$77-79m against H1 of ~$61.7m (Q1 actual $31.7m plus Q2 guide midpoint $30.0m) — a ~30% step-up in the quarterly run-rate that the CFO justified only as 'improve gradually in the second half of the year as we expect some efficiency gains' — and that FY OI guide had already been cut from $144-146m at the March print.
findings.adversary_note: Every input is published guidance and the arithmetic is a restatement of it. FY27 non-GAAP OI $139-141m and Q2 $29.5-30.5m are in the 2026-06-03 press release; Q1 actual $31.7m is in the same release; the $144-146m prior guide is in the 2026-03-11 release; the CFO's 'improve gradually in the second half of the year as we expect some efficiency gains' is in the published transcript. The cut was reported and the stock traded on it - CXM closed -3.03% on the print day and then bled from 5.45 to 4.91 by 2026-06-25, and ChartMill's headline that day was literally 'Falls on Soft Guidance Despite Q1 Beat.' Sprinklr also told the street WHY: lower services revenue, incremental AI investment, ViralMoment. And the H2 question is in the wire copy the day before the print: Investing.com's 2026-09-01 preview names 'profitability - management's ability to sustain margin expansion' and 'management's outlook for the second half of fiscal 2027' as two of its three watch items, and puts the 9-analyst mean target at $7.88, i.e. 4% BELOW spot. That is a street that is not positioned for a raise. The only thing not published is the phrase '~30% step-up in the quarterly run-rate', which is division.

findings.finding: The Q2 FY27 revenue guide implies professional services of only ~$20.5m (total $214-215m less subscription $193.5-194.5m) versus actual PS of $24.7m, $27.2m and $28.8m in the last three quarters, and Sprinklr beat its own implied PS guide by 25% in Q3 FY26 ($28.8m actual vs $23.0m implied) and 10% in Q1 FY27 ($24.7m vs $22.5m implied) — so a headline revenue beat of roughly 1.5-2.5% is mechanically likely, but at the -10% PS gross margin management guided it adds nothing to operating income.
findings.adversary_note: The factual base is solid and I checked it: Q2 guide of $214-215m total against $193.5-194.5m subscription does imply ~$20.5m of PS, and the Q3 FY26 precedent is exact ($209-210m/$186-187m implied $23.0m PS versus $219.07m total less $190.3m subscription = $28.8m actual, +25%). So the mechanism is real and the sub-versus-PS decomposition of the beat is genuinely absent from the wire copy - that is why this is not a 90. But three things pull it down hard. First, the street already models the beat: FactSet consensus is $215.6m against a $214.5m guide midpoint, so ~$1m of it is in before you start. Second, the finding omits the counterweight from the same transcript it cites: management guided FY PS to ~$87m, about 10% of revenue and in line with the trailing three-year average, which is an explicit deliberate reset - $87m less $24.7m of Q1 leaves ~$20.8m per remaining quarter, so the 'low' Q2 implied PS is the plan, not an oversight. Third, and decisively for a one-day reaction, the finding does not resolve sign: exactly this pattern (headline beat, poor mix) produced +3.05% in December 2025 and -3.03% in June 2026. A claim that predicts a beat but not the reaction to it is not tradeable.

findings.finding: In the Q1 FY27 10-Q geographic disaggregation, Americas revenue FELL to $112.9m from $117.6m (-4.0% YoY) while 'Other' jumped to $29.6m from $15.9m (+86%), so 48.6% of revenue is now outside the Americas versus 42.8% a year earlier and 44% for FY26 — Sprinklr's home market is contracting and every dollar of growth is coming from the regions where the Middle East disruption and FX sit.
findings.adversary_note: The numbers are right - I pulled the disaggregation table and it reads Americas $112,861k versus $117,587k, EMEA $77,045k versus $72,036k, Other $29,573k versus $15,877k - and the observation that Sprinklr's home market is now shrinking while a small bucket carries all the growth is not in any wire copy. But it is published, in an indexed free filing-summary that specifically calls out 'Americas Revenue Decline: $112.9 million, down from $117.6 million,' dated the day the 10-Q was accepted, and twelve sell-side analysts have the segment table. That is the 20-40 band, not the 0-15 band. Two substantive problems with the interpretation rather than the fact. The linkage is loose: the finding says the growth is coming from 'the regions where the Middle East disruption and FX sit,' but the Middle East sits in EMEA, and 'Other' - the +86% bucket - is Asia-Pacific, so the two halves of the sentence describe different segments. And a small bucket nearly doubling (15.9 to 29.6) far more plausibly reflects a lumpy large deal or a reclassification than a genuine 86% regional growth rate, which the finding does not address. Mechanically, geography does not appear in the press release, only in the 10-Q filed days later, so this only surfaces tomorrow morning if an analyst asks.

findings.finding: The Q1 FY27 10-Q discloses that 'our operations in the Middle East have been affected by the 2026 Iran conflict, including disruptions to our business activities in the region and inaccessibility, and potential loss, of certain customer data in connection with a third-party data center infrastructure in the United Arab Emirates' and warns of 'significant and unanticipated expenses... emergency data transfers, temporary changes to data processing locations, increased infrastructure costs' — and the conflict's targeting of Gulf data centres was still live in July 2026, i.e. across the whole of the quarter being reported (1 May - 31 July 2026).
findings.adversary_note: The quoted language is verbatim accurate - I confirmed it in the filing. But every element of the exposure has been public since 2026-06-04 and, critically, management already SIZED it on the record that day: 'about $3 million to $4 million of slip deals that could have closed in the quarter' plus 'we had to move 54 customers on the fly out of a damaged cloud infrastructure environment in the Middle East to Ireland.' That is in the published transcript, and the 10-Q's UAE data-centre sentence appears in the indexed StockTitan summary of the filing. The 2026 Iran war is one of the most heavily covered stories of the year, so 'the conflict was still live across the quarter' is not a discovery. On magnitude: $3-4m is 1.4-1.9% of a $214.5m quarter, it is what happened LAST quarter, and the company still beat revenue and posted a $31.7m OI. Management characterised the region as having 'a very healthy pipeline' with 'several very large deals over the next 2, 3 quarters.' So a repeat of the same headwind is inside the guide's own experience, not a shock to it.

findings.finding: The scheduled termination date of Sprinklr's $125m variable-tenor accelerated share repurchase with Citibank is September 1, 2026 — today, the session before the print — after which the dealer's covering purchases (roughly $125m spread over ~115 sessions on a 2.76m-share ADV) stop, and only $75m of the $200m authorization remains through 15 March 2027.
findings.adversary_note: I verified the date in the filing itself, verbatim: 'The scheduled termination date is September 1, 2026,' with $125m paid to Citibank on 2026-03-16, an initial delivery of 17,123,288 shares, and $75m of the $200m authorization remaining. So the fact is correct and the finding is right that it is obscure. Three things cap it at the middle of the range. First, it IS published, and not only in the footnote - an indexed filing summary of the same 10-Q states the September 1, 2026 scheduled termination date on 2026-06-04, and the $200m programme with a ~$125m ASR intention was disclosed in the 2026-03-11 8-K and covered as 'starts $200M share repurchase plan.' Second, the same disclosure says Citibank may terminate the ASR EARLY at its discretion, which neither this finding nor its twin mentions - so 'the buying stops today' is not established; it may have stopped weeks ago and there is no filing that would tell us. Third and most important: this is a flow claim, not an earnings claim. By the finding's own arithmetic the dealer's covering is ~$1.09m/day against ~$19m/day of dollar volume, i.e. ~6% of the bid. Removing 6% of one buyer does not set a print-day gap; the release does. A mechanical buyer ending is a fact about the days after tomorrow.

findings.finding: Sprinklr's $125m accelerated share repurchase with Citibank has a stated scheduled termination date of September 1, 2026 - the last session before the print - so the dealer's programmatic buying of roughly 21m shares (about 6-7% of the 2.76m-share ADV every day since 11 March) ends exactly as the event begins; the stock's 54% advance from $5.32 on 1 July to $8.21 on 31 August came in near-daily 1-3% increments with no news gap, and CXM was quoted down 3.3% at $7.94 on 2026-09-01 itself, the ASR's termination date.
findings.adversary_note: This is the same claim as CXM-a#5 off the same filing, and I accept the date. What I reject is the causal attribution, which is the part that would make it information - and I reject it on the tape, not on principle. (a) The ASR has been running since 2026-03-16, so if its covering bid were setting the price it was setting it while CXM fell from 6.01 on 2026-06-01 to 4.91 on 2026-06-25 and made 52-week-low territory. (b) The finding's own sizing sinks it: ~6-7% of a 2.76m-share ADV cannot produce a 54% advance. (c) 'No news gap' is false on the bars I pulled: 2026-08-27 closed 7.94 against 7.47 the prior session, +6.3% in one day, and the whole 20-day advance is concentrated in the second half of August. (d) There is an obvious alternative cause the finding does not consider, and it is enormous: the S&P software index gained roughly 14% in August 2026, its strongest August in data back to 1990, with IGV up over 16%, while CXM's own August was +25.9% (6.52 area on 2026-08-03 to 8.21 on 2026-08-31) - entirely consistent with a high-beta small-cap participating in a sector melt-up. (e) CXM-specific news exists too: the 2026-08-13 appointment of Microsoft's President of Search & AI to the board, covered by Barchart, Globe and Mail, TipRanks, Investing.com and citybiz, effective 2026-08-17, the exact session from which the advance accelerates (6.70 -> 7.40 by 08-21). (f) The 'quoted down 3.3% at $7.94' is overstated: 8.21 to the baseline's 7.9955 is -2.6%, and the intraday print I read was 8.065. Finally, like a#5, the mechanism is flow after the print, not content of the print.

findings.finding: The quarter being reported (1 May - 31 July 2026) was run without a Chief Revenue Officer for two of its three months: Scott Millard resigned effective 2025-11-11 after roughly seven weeks in the job, Tom Addis did not start until 2026-07-01, and SVP Global Sales Kevin Connolly left for NewRocket in the same window - so tomorrow's Q3 guide is the first ever set by a revenue chief with two months of tenure.
findings.adversary_note: Every dated element is in published wire copy on its own day and the vacancy is arithmetic from two press releases. Millard's departure effective 2025-11-11 was reported on 2025-11-07 by StreetInsider, TipRanks, Investing.com and MarketScreener; Addis's start on 2026-07-01 was an 8-K plus a press release carried by TradingView, Globe and Mail, Yahoo and StockTitan. The wider fact - that Sprinklr has churned its CFO, its CRO twice and senior sales leadership inside twelve months - is a standard, much-repeated part of the bear case on this name, and the market has already seen what soft guidance from this management does to the stock (-3.03% on 2026-06-03 and a slide to 4.91 within three weeks). I could not verify the Kevin Connolly / NewRocket leg at all, so that piece is unsupported as written. And the sign is not established: a CRO with two months of tenure is at least as likely to set a deliberately beatable Q3 bar as an unachievable one, and the finding's own framing ('the first ever guide set by a revenue chief with two months of tenure') is rhetoric about a fact that has been public since 2026-07-01.

findings.finding: The Iran-Gulf war, which Sprinklr's 10-Q says caused 'inaccessibility, and potential loss, of certain customer data' at a third-party UAE data centre and which management sized on 4 June as $3-4m of slipped deals plus 54 customers force-migrated to Ireland, escalated again INSIDE the reported quarter (Iranian missiles and drones fired at Gulf states on 2026-07-12) and hostilities resumed on 2026-08-31 - against a guide that assumed 'improvements in the coming quarters', with 44% of FY26 revenue generated outside the Americas.
findings.adversary_note: Dates check out off the URL paths: the Al Jazeera piece is /2026/7/12/ and reports Iranian missiles and drones engaged by UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain, and the 2026-08-31 event is documented as the first confirmed Iranian strike on a Gulf-region state since the July resumption, with a drone engaged by the UAE. So the escalation inside the reported quarter is real. But this is the same 10-Q sentence and the same management sizing as CXM-a#4, and both halves are published: the $3-4m of slipped deals and the 54 customers moved to Ireland are on the 2026-06-04 call, and the Iran war has been front-page globally all year. The exposure framing is also inflated. '44% of FY26 revenue generated outside the Americas' is not Middle East exposure - the Middle East is a sub-slice of EMEA, which management placed 'upper middle' among twelve geographies with good performance despite the headwinds. And the market's own answer is on the tape: CXM closed UP at 8.21 on 2026-08-31, the day hostilities resumed. Against a quarter guided to $214.5m, a repeat of the disclosed $3-4m is 1.4-1.9% of revenue - real, but the same order as last quarter's, which the company absorbed and still beat.

findings.finding: The 13 August 8-K appointing Microsoft's President of Search & AI, Jordi Ribas, states explicitly that there are no related-party arrangements, family relationships or reportable transactions, and seats him on the Nominating & Corporate Governance and Strategy committees - i.e. it is governance, not a Microsoft commercial relationship - while the same filing shows the board's Strategy Committee was converted from ad hoc to standing at the 2026 annual meeting.
findings.adversary_note: This is the highest priced-in item in the brief almost by construction: the source IS the document everybody reported, and the framing it argues for is the framing every outlet already used. On 2026-08-13 Barchart, Globe and Mail ('Sprinklr Adds Microsoft AI Leader to Board of Directors'), TipRanks, Yahoo, Investing.com, citybiz and Simply Wall St all carried it as a board/AI-expertise appointment, and Simply Wall St explicitly read it as deepening board-level AI expertise. No publication I can find claimed a Microsoft commercial relationship, so this finding negates a narrative that was never in the price - which is agreement with the wire, not information. I also could not verify one of its assertions: the 8-K I read contains the related-party and family-relationship language verbatim and the two committee seats, but it says nothing about the Strategy Committee being converted from ad hoc to standing at the 2026 annual meeting; what it does say is that Eileen Schloss was removed from that committee effective 2026-08-17. So that leg is unsupported as written.

findings.finding: The market paid +12.84% in one session (close 339.31 on 26 Aug to 382.85 on 27 Aug 2026) for nothing but a StreetInsider rumour that PANW is circling Cribl ($3.5bn) and ClickHouse ($15bn) - yet every time PANW has actually announced a deal the stock has been sold: -14% over two days on the CyberArk announcement (30 Jul 2025) and -7.42% the session after the 19 Nov 2025 print at which Chronosphere was announced alongside a double beat.
findings.adversary_note: Both halves of this finding are in same-day pre-print wire copy, and the causal half is also wrong. (a) Causation: the +12.83% on 2026-08-27 (339.31 -> 382.85, verified) was NOT 'nothing but a StreetInsider rumour'. CrowdStrike reported after the close on 2026-08-26, beat and raised on AI-threat-driven demand; on 08-27 CRWD had its best day ever (+20%) and Okta +29%, and CNBC's sector piece explicitly lists 'Palo Alto Networks, SailPoint, Zscaler and Rubrik up at least 10% each' on that rally. The Cribl/ClickHouse item was a co-driver at most, and the Motley Fool retail explainer the hunter cites is the weakest available source on attribution. (b) Even taking the momentum-premium framing at face value, the premium has already come out INSIDE the sealed baseline: Aug 31 close 382.13 vs baseline spot 363.995 at 14:07 UTC = -4.7% today, and the Fool's own 2026-09-01 piece attributes today's -4.9% to pre-earnings profit-taking on a doubled EV/EBITDA multiple. (c) The reaction-function half is verified but published. I confirmed the price facts independently (Yahoo daily bars: 2025-07-28 204.50 -> 07-30 183.03 = -10.5% two-day, -> 07-31 173.60 = -15.1% three-day, so '-14% over two days' is loose but the substance holds; 2025-11-19 199.90 -> 11-20 185.07 = -7.42% exactly; 2026-02-17 163.50 -> 02-18 152.35 = -6.82% exactly). But Investing.com, published 2026-09-01 BEFORE this print, states 'Four consecutive beats. Three consecutive sell-offs', average post-earnings move ~-5.2%, range -6.67% to -8.75%, AND 'PANW surged +10.39% on August 27 - just days before earnings. The stock has already moved as if it beat.' That is this finding, both legs, in today's preview copy. The finding also omits the fourth data point (the 2026-06-02 Q3 print, ~-8.5%), which the published pattern includes. On the skew: I rule that the -17.1 call-bid skew here is NOT the market dismissing a known selloff pattern - the pattern is in today's copy and analysts still sit 41-of-54 Strong Buy - it is the market paying for a genuine two-sided AI-security demand upcycle validated 96 hours ago by CRWD and OKTA. Cheap puts here are cheap because the sector tape turned, not because a risk went unread.

findings.finding: Tonight's first-ever FY27 EPS guide has to be built on roughly 9-10% more shares than the FY26 base: PANW's own Q3 FY26 release guides FY26 diluted shares to 763-766m but Q4 alone to 830-840m, and PANW has already cut its own FY26 EPS guide once on this exact mechanism (from $3.80-3.90 to $3.65-3.70 on 17 Feb 2026, on deal costs that more than doubled), a print after which the stock closed -6.82%.
findings.adversary_note: I accept every fact here - I checked each one against the company's own releases and they are exactly right - and reject the novelty. Verified: Q3 FY26 release (SEC-filed, 2026-06-02) guides FY26 diluted non-GAAP EPS $3.77-$3.79 on 763-766m shares and Q4 FY26 $0.96-$0.98 on 830-840m shares; Q2 FY26 release (2026-02-17) guided FY26 to $3.65-$3.70 on 768-773m, down from the Q1 FY26 release (2025-11-19) $3.80-$3.90 on 710-716m; and the 2026-02-18 reaction was -6.82% (163.50 -> 152.35). So the arithmetic is clean and the ~9-13% FY27 share-count step-up is real. But every input is in a filed 8-K exhibit that has been public for three months, and the implication is already in consensus: FY27 consensus EPS is $3.98 against FY26 guidance of $3.77-$3.79 - only +5% EPS growth against consensus FY27 revenue of $13.8bn, i.e. +21%. That 16-point wedge IS the dilution plus deal financing; sell-side has modelled it. The 112m shares issued to CyberArk holders and a '13.5% dilution of existing EPS' have been published since the 2025-07-30 announcement. Two further problems with sign and size. First, the mechanism the finding treats as a one-way ratchet already reversed once: on 2026-06-02 PANW raised FY26 EPS back to $3.77-$3.79 on a LOWER full-year share count (763-766 vs 768-773), so the Feb cut was not a durable dilution story. Second, and more important, EPS is demonstrably not this stock's decision variable. PANW went from 141.67 (2026-02-24) to a 52-week high near 396 - roughly 2.8x - across the same period its FY26 EPS guide was being cut, and every pre-print preview I found says the number that decides tonight is the initial FY27 NGS ARR guide against a FactSet-implied ~22% / $10.9bn bar, not the EPS line. On the brief's consensus-equals-guidance test: it is true (Q4 consensus $0.98 on $3.35bn vs guide $0.96-$0.98 on $3.345-3.355bn) but it is also the ordinary state of a guidance-anchored name and is itself published in today's Investing.com preview, so it does not make the FY27 guide unanchored - the FY27 anchor is public and numeric.

findings.finding: PANW's GSA OneGov agreement gives every federal agency up to 60% off list on designated bundles of Prisma AIRS Runtime Security, VM-Series software firewalls, Panorama/CDSS, Prisma SASE and Prisma Browser (35% on Code to Cloud) through 31 Jan 2028 - and PANW's fiscal Q1 FY27, the quarter it guides tonight, is the first US federal year-end (30 Sep) buying quarter to run entirely under that pricing.
findings.adversary_note: I accept the fact and reject the sign. The fact is precisely stated and I verified every element against the GSA release itself (URL path ...onegov-12042025, body dated 2025-12-04): 60% off list on designated bundles of Prisma AIRS Runtime Security and VM-Series software firewalls including Panorama and Cloud Delivered Security Services; 60% on Prisma Access Enterprise (SASE and Prisma Browser); 35% on CNAPP / Code to Cloud; available through 2028-01-31. And the calendar claim holds: PANW's fiscal Q1 FY27 runs 2026-08-01 to 2026-10-31, contains the 2026-09-30 federal year-end, and is the first such quarter under pricing that only began 2025-12-04. That is careful work. The problem is direction. (i) These are discounts off LIST, and PANW's realised federal pricing already ran at large discounts through GSA schedules and Carahsoft; the incremental erosion versus realised ASPs is a small fraction of 60%. (ii) OneGov is structurally a volume-for-price trade - GSA's own framing is adoption acceleration - and on subscription products a Sep-quarter federal surge lands in NGS ARR and RPO, which is exactly the metric every preview says decides tonight, not in the revenue line. (iii) The empirical test already ran: the agreement has been live across three full PANW quarters (Q2 FY26 Nov-Jan, Q3 FY26 Feb-Apr, Q4 FY26 May-Jul) and PANW raised FY26 revenue guidance in both February and June and guides Q4 NGS ARR to +59-60% - if OneGov were compressing federal economics it would already show. (iv) Size: US federal is a minority vertical for an $11.4bn revenue base; even an aggressive read on incremental discount depth is well under 1% of revenue. So the mechanism reaches the print, but I score the sign as positive-to-neutral, not negative. On publication: this sits between the 20-40 and 45-65 anchors - GSA.gov, Nextgov, MeriTalk and ExecutiveGov all carried it in December 2025, which is public but not financial press, and one equity outlet (Simply Wall St, 2025-12-14) discussed it and still framed margin pressure as coming from acquisition integration rather than federal pricing. Nine months old, on the wire, never quantified, and never linked to this print. Hence 55.

findings.finding: MongoDB's contracted remaining performance obligation stood at $1,458.6m at 30 Apr 2026 against $774.3m a year earlier (+88%) while revenue grew 25%, with the duration lengthening (53% due in the next 12 months vs 58% a year ago; 46% in 13-36 months vs 38%) and non-current deferred revenue up from $24.3m to $91.2m — so committed next-12-month revenue rose roughly 72% YoY, a visibility base far larger than the market's pure 'Atlas consumption' framing assumes and the main reason a bigger-than-usual FY27 raise is mechanically available.
findings.source_date: 2026-04-30 (period end; reported in the 10-Q at https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001441816/000162828026039150/mdb-20260430.htm, prior-year figure at https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1441816/000144181625000118/mdb-20250430.htm)
findings.adversary_note: The facts are right and the arithmetic essentially checks, but this is not an XBRL/10-Q discovery at all — MongoDB put the entire package in its own Q1 FY27 earnings press release on 2026-05-28: 'RPO $1,458.6 million, up 88% year-over-year', 'cRPO $766.3 million, up 69% year-over-year', and non-current deferred revenue $91.2 million are all headline line items in that release, and the CFO quantified it verbally on the call ('ended the period at $1.46 billion... year over year growth of 88% with the current portion growing'). Wire copy carried it as 'backlog up 88%'. The hunter's derived '+72% next-12-month committed revenue' is in fact a slightly worse restatement of a company-disclosed +69% cRPO, computed from the duration-mix percentages rather than the disclosed dollar figure. More damaging for the mechanism: the FY27 raise the finding says is 'mechanically available' has already happened — the same 2026-05-28 release lifted FY27 to $2.92-2.96bn WITH the +88% RPO in hand, and the stock moved +3.03%. The market has seen this exact backlog number alongside a raise and repriced for it; the subsequent +23% 20-day and +32% one-month run-up on AI-workload momentum, with targets lifted to $475 (Truist) and $525 (Evercore), means the strong-visibility read is now the consensus going in, not the variant. The only sliver not drawn out anywhere is the 10-Q duration-mix footnote (46% in 13-36 months vs 38%), i.e. that the lengthening is where the growth sits — worth a few points off 100, no more. Note also management's own caveat that 'it remains difficult to predict the duration of our EA deals', which cuts against treating RPO as a clean forward multiplier for a consumption business.

findings.finding: The quarter being reported (fiscal Q2, May-July 2026) is precisely MongoDB's go-to-market handover quarter: incoming CRO Ryan Mac Ban started 27 Apr 2026 and the 24 Mar 2026 release states 'Outgoing CRO Paul Capombassis will support a seamless transition to Mac Ban through Q2', while the President of Field Operations, Cedric Pech, resigned effective 15 Apr 2026 and product leadership was split into two new Chief Product Officers on 22 Apr 2026 — i.e. a full field-and-product leadership rebuild landing inside the reported quarter, with a new CEO only ten months in.
findings.adversary_note: Every component of this is published, most of it in wire copy, and one component moved the price by 22% on the day it landed. Cedric Pech's resignation was disclosed in the 8-K filed 2026-03-02 — the same 8-K as the Q4 FY26 Item 2.02 results, i.e. the print the baseline records at -22.24%; so the market's single largest negative MDB reaction in eight events already had the field-leadership departure inside it. The Mac Ban appointment and the exact 'Capombassis will support a seamless transition to Mac Ban through Q2' language went out on PR Newswire, Reuters and Investing.com on 2026-03-24. The two new CPOs were named on 2026-04-22 and re-narrated by management on the 2026-05-28 call. The finding's *mechanism* has also been written out explicitly in public: Simply Wall St's April note says leadership transitions at the top of sales 'can lead to short term disruption in deal cycles, territory alignment, or sales incentives, which may affect how quickly MongoDB converts AI related interest into signed contracts', and TheStreet's 2026-05-20 BofA piece states that the simultaneous CRO and President-Field-Operations departures 'added to investor concern about near-term sales execution' and that this combination helped drive a 20% YTD decline. And management pre-empted the specific risk on the record on the Q1 call: 'we felt very confident in terms of making sure that there was not going to be any... changes to comp plans... I would not expect any significant changes for the remainder of fiscal 2027'. Where I stop short of 90: I accept the fact and I accept the sign is at least available, but I found no piece that assembles the four moves into 'the quarter being reported IS the handover quarter' and prices it, and nobody has quantified it. That aggregation is a real, if thin, edge. I do not accept the size implied by framing it as a full 'field-and-product leadership rebuild' — the outgoing CRO stayed on through the quarter by design, the new CRO started 27 Apr with the quarter's pipeline already built, and the sign is genuinely two-sided: a handover quarter is as often sandbagged into a beatable guide as it is missed.

findings.finding: In a Reg FD 8-K furnished 2026-07-08, GitLab restated the Duo Agent Platform paid Consumption Run Rate it had touted five weeks earlier as 'nearly $20 million' down to approximately $15 million, because the calculation 'now excludes certain one-time credit incentives granted to paying customers' - i.e. roughly a quarter of the headline AI number the street heard in June was credits given away to existing paying seats, not incremental purchase.
findings.adversary_note: The 'hard to machine-read JPEG deck' argument fails for this specific claim, because the restatement language is not in the deck at all - it is in the plain HTML body of the 8-K itself. I fetched the filing and it reads, in text, 'nearly $20 million' / 'closer to $15 million' / 'the calculation now excludes certain one-time credit incentives granted to paying customers' / 'surpassed $20 million as of June 30, 2026', and in the same breath the company states CRR 'is not material to the Company's financial performance at this time'. StockTitan headlined it 'GitLab updates CRR and Q1 FY27 metrics' and TradingView carried it on the same day, both spelling out the downward revision and both reasons (add Flex, drop one-time incentives). Decisively, the market saw the restatement and the >$20M print together on 2026-07-08 and took the stock UP 7.8%, and DA Davidson raised its target on consumption trends off the same document. So the fact is public, connected to exactly this metric, and has already had its price day - and the day went the other way. I hold back from 90+ only because the mainstream copy (TipRanks, Globe and Mail) omitted the $15M entirely and led with '>$20M', so the hunter's specific framing - that ~a quarter of the June AI headline was giveaway credits to existing paying seats rather than incremental purchase - is drawn out nowhere in the wire. The fact is fully priced; the implication is under-drawn. Size is also small on the company's own arithmetic: $5M of a $20M CRR is 0.45% of the $1,112-1,118M FY27 revenue guide.

findings.finding: GitLab's FY27 guidance explicitly embeds no material Duo Agent Platform revenue contribution, yet the company went out of its way one month into Q2 to confirm paid CRR had gone from ~$15M at 30 April to above $20M at 30 June on the same restated basis - a ~33% step-up in two months on a line that is upside-only versus the guide.
findings.adversary_note: This is not an unpriced positive - it is the consensus bull case and it is the literal headline of the 2026-07-08 Business Update. Every wire item I can find leads with exactly this sentence: TipRanks, Globe and Mail, TradingView and StockTitan all report 'paid Consumption Run Rate surpassed $20 million as of June 30, 2026' on the restated basis. The same release also disclosed 'more than 100% year-over-year growth in first orders so far in the second quarter'. The stock rose 7.8% on it and the sell side re-rated: DA Davidson raised on consumption trends off this document, and August brought target raises to $45-$52 across DA Davidson, Cantor, BTIG, TD Cowen, Truist, UBS and BofA. The 'upside-only versus the guide' half of the claim is also a restatement of published guidance, not a discovery - GitLab's own 8-K says CRR 'is not material to the Company's financial performance at this time', which is the company telling you in writing that the guide does not lean on it. This is the 90-100 anchor almost by definition: consensus plus restated guidance. I checked the one thing that could rescue it - whether the street models a beat - and consensus revenue of $273.13M sits inside the $272-274M Q2 guide, essentially at the midpoint, which is a mildly supportive setup fact but is itself mechanically published and not a Duo-specific insight. The positive-fighting-a-positioned-market argument does apply here in the hunter's favour: with puts bid at +6.53 vol points and a 14.37% implied move, an upside surprise is the less-hedged tail. That is worth a few points of discount, not more, because the specific fact cited is already in the spot.

findings.finding: GitLab 19.3, released 2026-08-20, made hard GitLab Credits usage caps generally available - subscription-level and per-user spend ceilings after which 'features that consume GitLab Credits, like GitLab Duo Agent Platform, are suspended until the next billing period' - and the same release cycle added a GitLab Dedicated AI Gateway letting enterprises connect their own inference models; both are direct concessions to customers who in GitLab's own public forum call the credit economics 'fundamentally broken' (one reported ~$10 of credits consumed by a single agentic task).
findings.adversary_note: I accept the facts and reject both the reach and the confidence in the sign. Every hard fact here is in a GitLab press release dated 2026-08-20 carried on StockTitan - not a docs page: 'GitLab Credits usage caps are now generally available, allowing organizations to set a monthly ceiling on agentic AI spend before it becomes an overage', Dedicated AI Gateway 'generally available', and customers can 'connect their own models for inference'. That is wire copy, so the 'obscure release note' premise does not hold. Two further problems. First, mechanism: GitLab's Q2 FY27 ended 2026-07-31, and 19.3 shipped 2026-08-20 - twenty days after the close. Caps cannot touch the reported quarter and can only reach forward CRR commentary, and even that is on a line the company itself calls immaterial ($20M CRR is 1.8% of the $1,112-1,118M FY27 guide). Second, the sign: the negative reading is the hunter's, not the document's. Spend caps, per-user limits and BYO-inference are the standard enterprise-procurement checklist for every consumption vendor, GitLab framed them as scaling agentic AI into regulated enterprises, and the tape did not treat them as a concession - the August news flow coincided with target raises to $45-$52. The docs wording 'features... are suspended until the next billing period' is a mechanical description of any spend cap, not evidence of demand distress. I also could not verify the load-bearing colour: I searched the GitLab forum and found an 'Expensive AI' thread and pricing grumbles, but no post calling the credit economics 'fundamentally broken' and no ~$10-per-agentic-task report. So the unpublished part of this finding is an interpretation resting on a quote I cannot confirm. Where the hunter does earn credit: the specific inversion - that a GA spend ceiling structurally caps the growth rate of the exact metric the equity is being bid on - is genuinely not drawn out anywhere I can find, and with puts bid at +6.53 vol points there is a market already willing to pay for that story.

findings.finding: The scope of the credits wallet - and therefore of the CRR metric the market is treating as an AI-adoption gauge - is being broadened beyond AI: GitLab Secrets Manager is now 'an add-on billed through GitLab Credits' (19.3, 2026-08-20) and GitLab's own docs repository carries a commit dated 2026-08-26 titled 'Broaden GitLab Credits scope beyond Duo Agent Platform', on top of the CRR definition already having been changed once in July to add Flex and drop one-time incentives.
findings.adversary_note: Half fact, half over-read, and the fact half is in a press release. I verified the git log directly: the commit 'Broaden GitLab Credits scope beyond Duo Agent Platform' exists on doc/subscriptions/gitlab_credits.md and is dated 2026-08-26, exactly as claimed - so the hunter's sourcing is honest. But the commit's own message defeats the inference: the author notes 'the page opened by saying credits are used for GitLab Duo Agent Platform, while the dashboard section of the same page already lists Secrets Manager as a credit-consuming product.' That is a wording-consistency fix to a docs page that had fallen behind the product, not a change to a disclosed metric. The substantive fact - Secrets Manager billed through Credits - was published in GitLab's own 2026-08-20 press release ('now in limited availability as a paid add-on billed through GitLab Credits'), which is wire copy, and the CRR definition change (add Flex, drop one-time incentives) was published in the 2026-07-08 8-K and reported by StockTitan and TradingView the same day. What is left that is genuinely new is only the leap: that CRR is therefore being diluted as an AI-adoption gauge. I reject that as stated, on two grounds. There is no published evidence that Secrets Manager revenue is inside CRR - CRR's scope is set by IR disclosure, not by a docs page - and Secrets Manager was only in limited availability as of 2026-08-20, after the 2026-07-31 quarter close, so it cannot be inside a July-31 CRR figure. So the mechanism does not reach tonight's number. It is a real forward disclosure-quality risk on a metric the company itself calls immaterial, which caps the size regardless. I am not going higher than 60 because the specific argument - that the market's AI gauge is quietly becoming a mixed-product gauge - is nowhere in the published commentary, and that framing is the finding's only unpriced content.
